# Plots and tables {#sec-plots}

The package draws the paper's figures and tables from its own output: estimate tables from
`sc_estimate()`, fitted laws from `sc_fitted_law()` and posterior summaries from `sc_posterior()`.
The functions use base graphics, so `layout()` or `par(mfrow = )` combine several calls into one
figure. Each returns the data it drew, invisibly, so you can check what is on the page. The examples
use the toy fit of @sec-quantities and run in seconds. Their estimates mean nothing.

```{r}
#| label: p-setup
library(sconjoint)
toy <- sc_load(system.file("extdata", "toy_fit.rds", package = "sconjoint"))
f <- paste0("tax", 1:6, "_linear")            # the linear term of each bracket's rate
bn <- c("Below $10k", "$10-35k", "$35-85k", "$85-175k", "$175-375k", "Above $375k")
dem <- function(g) g$party == "Dem"
means <- sc_estimate(toy, lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_mean(bn[j], f[j])))
means_dem <- sc_estimate(toy, lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_mean(bn[j], f[j], w = dem)))
shares <- sc_estimate(toy, lapply(1:6, function(j) sc_share(bn[j], f[j])), bounded = FALSE)
laws <- lapply(f, function(cc) sc_fitted_law(toy, cc))
```

## Estimates

`sc_plot_estimates()` draws one row per target: a point for the estimate and a line for its 95%
interval. It takes one or more estimate tables. Several tables, passed as named arguments, become
groups in different colors, with the names in the legend. Key arguments: `labels` and `order` for
the rows, `scale = 100` for percent, `xlim`, `reference` for values to compare with (true values
in a simulation, regression AMCEs) and `hide_wide` to drop intervals that span almost all of
$[0, 1]$. A point is hollow when its interval is missing. `plot()` on an estimate table calls the
same function.

```{r}
#| label: p-estimates
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.6
sc_plot_estimates(All = means, Democrats = means_dem)
```

@fig-sim-estimates compares estimates with the truth, and @fig-gs-compensation and
@fig-br-party-shares show three groups.

## Fitted laws

`sc_plot_laws()` draws fitted laws from `sc_fitted_law()`. With `layout = "ridges"` (the default)
the laws share one panel, one row each, scaled to the same height. With `layout = "panels"` each law
gets its own panel, and `means` adds the corrected mean as a red line with its 95% interval as a red
bar. `truth` takes true density functions in a simulation. The curves are fitted values before the
one-step correction, so a corrected mean need not sit at a curve's center. (In the toy fit the
corrected means fall outside the curves, so the example leaves them out.)

```{r}
#| label: p-laws
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.8
sc_plot_laws(laws[c(1, 6)], labels = bn[c(1, 6)], layout = "panels", ncol = 2)
```

@fig-gs-distributions-1 and @fig-br-distributions use panels with means, and @fig-sim-laws
adds the truth.

## Summary figure

`sc_plot_preferences()` draws the paper's summary figure, one row per feature: (A) the mean taste,
(B) its fitted law as a ridge, (C) the share with a positive taste, in percent, and, with `ames`,
(D) the choice effect in percentage points, with optional `reference` values as grey diamonds. Key
arguments: `order` for the rows, and `xlim`, `ticks` and `titles`, each a list named by panel. In
Panel C, `hide_wide` hides intervals that span at least 95 points.

```{r}
#| label: p-preferences
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 2.6
sc_plot_preferences(means, laws, shares, order = bn[c(1, 2, 6)])
```

@fig-gs-preferences and @fig-br-preferences are full examples.

## Importance

`sc_plot_importance()` draws importance shares as horizontal bars, in percent, with the value at
each bar's end. Each group is an estimate table of `sc_importance()` targets, passed as a named
argument. `combine` adds attributes into display groups. Names such as `"All.low"` lose the
common prefix, so rows of different tables match by attribute.

```{r}
#| label: p-importance
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
fn <- toy$data$data$feature_names
g <- list(low = fn[1:4], middle = fn[5:8], high = fn[9:12], revenue = fn[13:16])
imp_all <- sc_estimate(toy, sc_importance(g, names = paste("All", names(g), sep = ".")),
                       bounded = FALSE)
imp_dem <- sc_estimate(toy, sc_importance(g, w = dem, names = paste("Dem", names(g), sep = ".")),
                       bounded = FALSE)
sc_plot_importance(All = imp_all, Democrats = imp_dem,
                   combine = list(rates = c("low", "middle", "high"), revenue = "revenue"))
```

@fig-gs-importance is the full example.

## Lines

`sc_plot_lines()` draws estimates against an ordered setting `x`, such as an income bracket: a line
with points for each table and a shaded band for the 95% intervals. Each table has one row per value
of `x`. `xlab` is required. `hline` sets the dashed reference line (default 0.5 for probabilities
and shares). One call draws one panel. For several panels, set up `layout()`, call the
function once per panel with `legend = FALSE`, and draw one legend.

```{r}
#| label: p-lines
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
sc_plot_lines(All = means, Democrats = means_dem, x = 1:6,
              xlab = "Income bracket (lowest to highest)")
```

@fig-gs-contests has three panels.

## Respondents

`sc_plot_posterior()` draws posterior summaries from `sc_posterior()`. Without `truth` it gives
respondents sorted by posterior mean, each with a 95% posterior interval. With `truth`, in a
simulation, it plots each posterior mean against the true value, with a 45-degree line and the
correlation. `which` picks the contrast.

```{r}
#| label: p-posterior
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.4
post <- sc_posterior(toy, contrasts = c(tax6_linear = 1), nodes = 256)
sc_plot_posterior(post, ylab = "Posterior taste for a higher top rate")
```

@fig-sim-posterior uses `truth`.

## Tables

`sc_table()` puts one or more estimate tables side by side: one row per target and one column per
table. A cell holds the estimate and its 95% interval (`style = "ci"`) or its standard error in
parentheses (`style = "se"`). `n = TRUE` adds the number of respondents. The output is a data frame,
a Markdown table or a LaTeX `tabular`.

```{r}
#| label: p-table
sc_table(All = means, Democrats = means_dem, digits = 3, n = TRUE)
```

In a Quarto or R Markdown chunk with `#| results: asis`, `format = "markdown"` prints as a table:

```{r}
#| label: p-table-md
#| results: asis
sc_table(All = means, Democrats = means_dem, digits = 3, format = "markdown")
```

`format = "latex"` returns a booktabs table for a paper. It escapes `%`, `&`, `_` and `#` in
labels and headers. Write other LaTeX special characters, such as `$`, as `\$` yourself.

```{r}
#| label: p-table-tex
sc_table(All = means, Democrats = means_dem, labels = paste("Bracket", 1:6), style = "se",
         format = "latex", caption = "Toy estimates")
```

@sec-gs and @sec-br each show one table at full scale.
